The spotted goatfish, Pseudupeneus maculatus, is a benthic reef dweller whose life history is closely tied to the warm, stable thermal regime of its Caribbean habitat. At a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a newly fertilized egg, measuring just one millimeter in diameter, develops rapidly; upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight of only 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], a mass that reflects the modest energy reserves contained within the small, pelagic ovum. This lecithotrophic phase is brief, and the rapid depletion of endogenous yolk soon necessitates the onset of exogenous feeding as the mouth opens and retinal differentiation enables prey detection. Field surveys of spawning aggregations indicate that females release their gametes in a broadcast event, producing approximately 72 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 72 eggs per spawning event], with spawning events occurring nearly daily during peak activity [F_R_i = events occurring nearly daily during peak activity], which together yield a daily reproduction rate of approximately 72 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 72 eggs per day], a strategy that maximizes the total number of propagules released into the planktonic environment.

Growth during the juvenile phase is comparatively rapid, though the species is not considered a large-bodied member of the Mullidae. Upon reaching sexual maturation, individuals typically achieve a fork length of about 18 centimeters [Lp = about 18 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. At this developmental milestone, the estimated wet weight of the fish is in the vicinity of 83.5 grams [Wwp = 83.5 grams], a body mass that supports the energetic demands of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. This weight is derived from length-weight regressions parameterized for the species, which indicate a robust allometric relationship between linear size and somatic mass. The attainment of this size and mass marks a clear transition from the pre-reproductive juvenile stage to the sexually mature adult phase, after which individuals are capable of participating in the annual spawning aggregations that characterize the species' reproductive biology in the Greater Antilles and along the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef.

The species exhibits a clear sexual size dimorphism that becomes evident as individuals approach their asymptotic dimensions. The ultimate fork length recorded for the spotted goatfish is 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a value that represents the upper boundary of somatic growth under favorable environmental conditions. Corresponding to this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 407 grams [Wwi = approximately 407 grams], a mass derived from the same length-weight power function used to estimate size at puberty. This asymptotic body size places Pseudupeneus maculatus among the mid-sized goatfishes of the western Atlantic, comparable in stature to the dory goatfish but notably smaller than the large-scale goatfish. The growth trajectory decelerates markedly after the inflection point near puberty, with the remaining mass gain directed primarily toward the accumulation of lipid reserves that are subsequently mobilized during the energetically costly spawning season. Such reserves are critical for sustaining the high metabolic demands of daily reproductive activity in warm waters.

Maximum longevity in this species has been documented under controlled conditions that replicate the thermal profile of its natural habitat. At a constant temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the observed lifespan reaches approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], which corresponds to about 2,190 days of sustained physiological function. This value is derived from captive-rearing studies that tracked individuals from the yolk-sac larval stage through senescence, monitoring the progressive deterioration of organ function that accompanies advanced age. In the wild, this lifespan is likely truncated by predation pressure and the energetic costs of repeated spawning events, yet the intrinsic physiological clock appears calibrated to this thermal regime. The species does not display the extreme post-reproductive senescence seen in some semelparous teleosts; instead, iteroparous adults may experience a gradual decline in fecundity and condition over their final years before succumbing to natural mortality.

Comparisons with congeneric species within the genus Pseudupeneus reveal that the spotted goatfish occupies an intermediate position in life-history space. The asymptotic length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] and a longevity of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] reflect a shift toward a slower pace of life compared to smaller relatives that mature at a fork length near 14 centimeters and exhibit a maximum lifespan of roughly four years at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. The reproductive strategy is similarly aligned: the maximum rate of 72 eggs per day [Ri = 72 eggs per day] is moderate when compared to the fecundity of large-bodied mullids, yet the nearly daily spawning frequency [F_R_i = nearly daily spawning frequency] compensates by ensuring continuous propagule output across the spawning season. This combination of moderate size, extended lifespan, and high-frequency reproduction at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] positions Pseudupeneus maculatus as a typical warm-water teleost whose life history is finely attuned to the predictable thermal environment of the Caribbean reef ecosystem. Further work on otolith microchemistry may help resolve whether regional variation in temperature modulates these demographic parameters across its range.
